claim: The Rubicon, a small river, marked the boundary between Caesar’s province and Italy; a general had to leave his army behind before crossing it.
In January 49 BCE Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army, starting a civil war.
Caesar is said to have declared “alea iacta est”: the die is cast.
Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in Greece in 48 BCE; Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered there.
“Crossing the Rubicon” now means passing a point of no return.
In 44 BCE Julius Caesar was made dictator for life.
On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate by conspirators led by Brutus and Cassius.
Marcus Brutus claimed descent from the Brutus who had expelled Rome’s last king.
The conspirators hoped to restore the Republic, but Caesar’s murder led to more civil war instead.
